messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 35
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: European
  relationship_status: Single
  occupation: Special Education Teacher
  trauma_type: Mugging or robbery
  pcl5: 58

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Shouting: Shouting, Somatic Pain (Neck): Neck pain, Authority Presence: Police
  Threat: Cannot Relax: I am unable to relax even when I know I am in a safe place, Flashbacks: Suddenly feeling or acting as if the stressful experience were actually happening again, Scanning Exits: I scan for exits as soon as I enter any room or building
  Memory: Photographic Recall: Remembering what happened during the frightening event is just like looking at photographs of it in my mind., Rage on Recall: When I remember the event I feel intense rage, Guilt on Recall: When I remember the event I feel intense guilt
  Negative Appraisals: Self-Comparison: Somebody else would not have gotten into this situation, Hypervigilance: I have to be on guard all the time, Inadequacy: I am inadequate

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Daniel Weber was 35 when he was mugged on his way home from school, where he worked as a special education teacher. It was early evening after a long day, and he had stayed late finishing paperwork and resetting materials for the next morning. On the walk to his car, he cut through a familiar stretch of sidewalk near the edge of the school grounds. He remembered hearing shouting before he fully understood it was directed at him. When he turned, two men were closing in. One demanded his wallet and phone, loudly, aggressively, in a way that Daniel still described in clipped, visual fragments rather than as a flowing story. What stayed with him was “like photographs”: the angle of one man’s face, the open mouth mid-yell, the flash of a hand grabbing at his jacket, the pavement rushing up as he was shoved. His neck twisted sharply when he hit the ground. He could recall the pressure there as distinctly as the images. He remembered freezing, fumbling, feeling slow. Even afterward, what burned in him was not only fear but rage—rage at being cornered, at being yelled at, at how exposed he had been—and, alongside it, a hard guilt that settled in almost immediately. He had come to believe somebody else would not have gotten into that situation, would have read the danger sooner, moved faster, done something more.

In the weeks after the robbery, Daniel returned to work, but the school no longer felt straightforwardly familiar. As soon as he entered any room or building, he found himself locating the exits before he could pay attention to anything else. In staff meetings he automatically chose seats near the door. In classrooms he noted where students, aides, and he himself could move if something went wrong. He did this even when he knew, logically, that he was safe. He was unable to relax in ordinary settings that had once been routine. During fire drills, raised voices in the hall, or moments when one student escalated and shouting broke out nearby, his body reacted before he could think. Sometimes he suddenly felt as if the robbery were happening again: the same jolt in his chest, the same narrowed attention, the sense that he was back on the pavement with someone yelling over him. At those moments he was not merely remembering; he was gripped by the immediacy of it.

The neck pain became its own kind of reminder. A stiffness at the base of his neck when he turned too quickly, an ache after a tense day, even the ordinary soreness that came from sleeping badly could pull him back to the moment of impact. He would feel the pain and instantly see one of those mental snapshots, vivid and still, followed by a rush of anger. He felt intense rage when the memory came, but the anger never stayed cleanly directed outward. It folded back into self-accusation. He was certain he had failed some basic test of competence. He compared himself harshly to an imagined other man who would have avoided the confrontation, taken another route, noticed the threat in time. The conclusion he kept reaching was that he was inadequate.

Police presence became difficult in a different way. When officers were visible around the school after neighborhood incidents or parked near a community event, Daniel stiffened. The sight of a uniform or patrol car pulled the robbery to mind with the same photographic quality, and with it came the whole charged mixture of helplessness, fury, and shame. He did not describe police as dangerous, but their presence marked the world as a place where something violent had already happened or could happen again. He felt he had to be on guard all the time.

Over months, these habits tightened around his daily life. He avoided lingering alone outside the school after dark and hurried colleagues along if they were chatting in the parking lot. He became less spontaneous socially and turned down invitations if they involved unfamiliar venues, partly because he wanted to know the layout before arriving. At work, where raised voices were not uncommon, he sometimes lost the thread of what a student or coworker was saying because he was tracking tone, volume, and doorways instead. He knew this made him seem distracted. For a man who took pride in being steady with vulnerable students, that stung. It fed the same private verdict: that he was not handling things the way he should.

By the time he sought help, Daniel was exhausted by the constant watchfulness. What finally pushed him to call was a recent incident at school when shouting in the hallway made him spin toward the door and brace as if he were back in the attack. He was shaken by how quickly it happened and by how visible it felt in front of others. Sitting in therapy, he spoke carefully, often in images rather than sequences, and rubbed the back of his neck while describing the robbery. What frightened him most was the sense that even safe places no longer felt safe in his body. What he hoped for was not to forget what happened, but to walk into his school, hear ordinary noise, see a police car outside, or feel a twinge in his neck without being thrown back into those frozen pictures of that evening.
